fullParagraphs: Takshashila University conferred honorary doctorates upon Tamil author and screenwriter S. Ramakrishnan and playback singer K.S. Chithra at its second convocation held at Ongur in Tindivanam recently.

articles.title: Man injured in crocodile attack near Chidambaram
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A 42-year-old man sustained minor injuries on his left thigh after being bitten by a crocodile that strayed into a house in Koppadi village near Chidambaram on Sunday.

According to police sources, P. Ilavarasan of Koppadi village was staying in his house when a dog began to bark continuously. When he went outside he was shocked to see a crocodile. The reptile lunged at him and attacked Ilavarasan on his left thigh. Hearing his cries, neighbours rushed to the spot and alerted the Forest Department.
Forest Department personnel arrived and, with the help of residents, safely captured the crocodile and released it into the Vakkaramari lake in Chidambaram.

articles.title: Pattabiram residents urge Highways dept. to build roundabouton CTH Road junction
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Residents of Pattabiram have urged the Highways Department to build a roundabout on the Chennai–Tiruvallur High Road (CTH) or Chennai–Tirupati–Renigunta Road near the flyover, replacing the Level Crossing 2 on the railway siding.
Without a roundabout, the six-way junction presents a chaotic sight during peak hours, said Roy Rozario, a resident.
Apart from the lanes of the C.T.H Road, road to/from Poonamallee and M.G. Road join the junction. People heading to the police station, TIDEL Park, hotels, schools, and colleges use the junction.

“Due to the lack of a roundabout, a lot of accidents happen as people drive on the wrong side of the road or drive recklessly. Long ago, the government had announced that a roundabout would be constructedat the location. We hope that it would come up soon,” he added.

Residents, meanwhile, have urged the department to open the other side of the flyover to traffic. “It has been completed. Only some works such as lighting, removal of excess cement concrete, and painting seem to remain. Though the surface is rough, people are driving on the incomplete side of the flyover to reach the other side,” said T. Sadagopan, activist.
The space beneath the flyover must also be cleared and the roads must be laid properly.

“Several bus services from Poonamallee, Thiruninravur, and other places have been cut, as there is no space to park the buses. Those buses that start from Pattabiram wait at random spots on the C.T.H Road. We want the Highways to also construct a foot overbridge beneath the flyover, or a limited-use subway,” said a resident.
Sources said the roundabout would be formed during the widening of the road. As far as a subway or a foot overbridge was concerned, necessary studies would be taken up.

articles.title: Six sent to juvenile home after Mumbai assault; Maharashtra SP leader seeks age change
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A juvenile court in Mumbai on Saturday sent six minors to a juvenile correctional home till December 4 in connection with the alleged assault of a couple at a garden in Kurla on Friday evening, police said on Sunday. The six are aged between 12 and 15, the Ghatkopar police said.

Deputy Commissioner of Police Ganesh Shinde said an FIR was lodged against the minors under Sections 189(2) (unlawful assembly), 118(1) (voluntarily causing hurt using dangerous weapons or means), 352 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace), and 351(2) (criminal intimidation) and other relevant provisions of the BNS.
All of them were produced before the Juvenile Justice Board and notices were sent to their parents.

According to the police, the couple was at the garden behind Phoenix Marketcity mall when a group of minors surrounded them and began to abuse them. When the couple tried to reason with the group, they assaulted them with a hockey stick and forced them out of the garden. Police detained them after a video of the incident surfaced on social media.
The police said they are recording the statements of the couple and the juveniles to determine whether the two groups had a dispute before the incident that took place at the Pramod Mahajan Garden.

The incident drew sharp reactions from political parties, with many condemning it. Samajwadi Party Maharashtra president Abu Asim Azmi said the juvenile age threshold should be brought down from 18 to 15 and that those below 18 years who commit murder, robbery or harassment should not be given concessions under the law. Mr. Azmi added that the incident should not be linked to religion and that the law should act without discrimination.
Meanwhile, BJP leader Kirit Somaiya met the couple at the Ghatkopar police station and promised action.

NCP (SP) MP Supriya Sule urged Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, who holds the Home portfolio, to “adopt a no-tolerance policy towards such incidents” and said citizens should be able to move around freely in the State.
Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Intekhab Farooqui also condemned the assault.

articles.title: Over 40% Group A posts vacant at PGIMS Rohtak, says former Minister
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Alleging that 41.6% of the sanctioned Group A posts at the Post-Graduate Institute of Medical Sciences (PGIMS) in Rohtak were lying vacant, former Haryana Home Minister Subhash Batra on Sunday questioned the BJP government’s claims of improving healthcare services in the State.

Citing an inspection by the Assembly’s Subject Committee in February, Mr. Batra said 424 of the 1,018 sanctioned Group A posts at the institute were vacant. He said the shortage of doctors, specialists and healthcare staff was affecting patient care at the institute, which catered to over 8,000 patients daily in its outpatient department.
Manjunath, in-charge of the Public Relations Department, PGIMS, did not respond to repeated calls and messages seeking his response to the former Minister’s allegations.

Addressing a press conference, Mr. Batra also pointed out that only 200 of the 540 medicines on the government-approved list were available in the hospital store during the Health Minister’s inspection in April. Supply orders for 172 types of medicines and surgical materials were pending with companies, he alleged.

Alleging that the “condition of the Radiology Department is also extremely concerning”, Mr. Batra said 10 of the 13 sanctioned faculty posts and nine of the 11 Senior Resident posts were vacant in the department, as per a September-October 2026 report. Of the nearly 500 patients advised ultrasound examinations daily, only 40% could undergo the test on the same day, he added.

Questioning the gap between budgetary allocations and the availability of health care facilities, Mr. Batra said ₹1,232 crore had been allocated to the Pandit Bhagwat Dayal Sharma University of Health Sciences and PGIMS for 2026-27, an increase of ₹422 crore over the previous year, but patients continued to face shortages of medicines and delays in diagnostic tests.
Mr. Batra also raised concerns over two incidents of ceiling plaster falling in the old hospital building in October.

On behalf of the Congress, Mr. Batra demanded that all vacant posts be filled, medicine stocks and pending complaints be made public, diagnostic facilities expanded and old hospital buildings subjected to a safety audit.

“The poor, labourers, farmers and the middle-class families in the State need doctors on time, essential medicines and quality treatment and not speeches and announcements,” he said, adding that the Congress would continue to raise this serious issue concerning health and hold the government accountable.

articles.title: Core accountability: On core sector performance
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The core sector performance in October is a good example of how statistical distortions can create incorrect assessments of the economy. The 10.9% growth rate, a series high, has been celebrated as a sign of the Indian economy’s strength and resilience. There is, no doubt, an aspect of this has been reflected in the numbers, especially to do with infrastructure creation. However, the much more impactful factor behind the high core sector growth was a low base effect. The overall Index of Core Industries grew just 0.8% in October 2025 and so, in relation, the performance in October 2026 looked that much faster. This low base effect is even starker when looking at individual sectors within the index. The coal sector grew at a blistering 23% in October, more than twice its growth rate in the previous month. Yet, a large part of this was propelled by the fact that the sector had contracted nearly 8.5% last October. The rest of the sector’s growth was driven by demand of the electricity and iron ore sectors, or so the data show. The electricity sector also grew at a series high of nearly 22% in October, but on the back of a near-7% contraction in October last year. This base effect anomaly is likely down to the fact that the festive season starts at different but similar points every year. As such, a more accurate reading of the economy will be possible once the data for November are available.

The construction-related sectors seem to have seen genuine growth, a reflection of the government’s ongoing infrastructure push. The iron ore sector’s growth rate accelerated to a three-month high of 26.4% in October 2026 as compared to a growth of 8.7% in the same month last year. Steel grew at 7.3% versus 9.5% last year, and cement by 15.4% versus 5.2%. The economy’s dependence on government spending is not going to ease in the near future, and might even intensify as higher costs eat into companies’ profit margins. The core sector data once again highlighted a major reason for these higher costs — the oil and gas sectors. The crude oil sector shrank by 4.1%, its 22nd consecutive month of contraction. The natural gas sector, similarly, contracted 7.6%, a series-worst performance and the 28th straight month of contraction. A major reason behind high inflation in India is the underperformance of these two sectors and the resultant dependence on imported fuel. It is time the Petroleum Ministry candidly explains — to Parliament in December or to the public directly — why India’s fuel output has been continuously falling. If it is a matter of a lack of resources underground, that is one thing, but the underperformance of oil and gas public sector undertakings is quite another. Accountability needs to be set.

articles.title: Rampur’s Lavi Fair: Storytelling through 300 years of Himalayan trade and tradition
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: What Disneyland is to children today, Lavi Fair in Rampur Bushahr, in Himachal Pradesh’s Shimla district, was to my family in the 1980s. I recall wandering through the fair as an eight-year-old, watching an old man smoking a chillum beside heaps of black sheep fleece and stacks of white woollen pattus (traditional garments of Kinnaur and Kullu women).

Mother and her friends carefully chose shawls for their daughters’ and future daughters-in-law’s trousseaux. Years later, I received a beautiful black sheep wool and pashmina shawl for my wedding. Wool finds pride of place at the fair. The name Lavi is linked to “Loe”, a sheet of woollen cloth and the practice of shearing sheep.

articles.title: Must balance ‘economic patriotism’ with cultural heritage: GJC on PM Modi’s call to stop gold purchases
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: While welcoming Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for prioritising locally-made products and reducing gold imports, the All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC) has said that India must balance “economic patriotism” and its cultural traditions when it comes to gold jewellery.

It argued that the sector contributes “nearly 7-8%” to the economy and supports “millions of livelihoods”. The GJC was reacting to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent and repeated appeal to all Indians to stop foreign trips and weddings, to buy local, and to only buy gold if necessary.

“The Prime Minister’s appeal for economic patriotism and greater preference for Swadeshi products is timely and welcome,” Rajesh Rokde, Chairman of the All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC) said.

“While we fully support the Prime Minister’s call for restraint when gold is viewed purely as bullion or an investment instrument, jewellery consumption remains closely linked to culture, craftsmanship, and livelihoods,” Mr. Rokde added.
He said that gold and jewellery hold a unique place in India’s cultural heritage, particularly during festive and wedding seasons, such as the period that India will soon enter in October-December.
“The jewellery industry, contributing nearly 7-8% to the economy and supporting millions of livelihoods, is an integral part of India’s growth story,” Mr. Rokde asserted.
‘People bought less gold, prices fell’: Modi recalls year-old appeal

“As a ₹10 lakh crore industry, the Indian jewellery sector must continue to grow responsibly, with greater transparency, value creation, and alignment with national priorities — balancing economic patriotism with India’s enduring cultural traditions,” he added.

articles.title: India, Finland seek to deepen economic ties through startup cooperation: Envoy Mikko Kivikoski
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: “India and Finland are looking to deepen economic cooperation by strengthening ties between their startup ecosystems and promoting greater two-way investment,” Finnish Ambassador to India Mikko Kivikoski has said.

"We want to engage more with the Indian startup actors. And of course, at the end of the day, this is all about advancing the economic cooperation between our countries. And here we see the startup sector, startup ecosystems, as an important part of that cooperation," Mr. Kivikoski told PTI .

The Ambassador was speaking at an unconventional startup event held at the Embassy of Finland in New Delhi on Friday (November 20, 2026), where entrepreneurs stepped into an ice-cold pool to pitch their ideas, drawing on Finland's winter-swimming tradition. "We have quite a long tradition in Finland for these kinds of events," Mr. Kivikoski said.

"This year has been record-high when it comes to interaction and engagement between Finland and India," he said, referring to visits by the Finnish Prime Minister and President, as well as meetings between the leaders of the two countries.

The Ambassador said the two sides agreed to elevate their bilateral relationship to a Strategic Partnership in Digitalisation and Sustainability during Finnish President Alexander Stubb's state visit to India in March.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi met his Finnish counterpart, Petteri Orpo, in New Delhi on the sidelines of the AI Impact Summit in February and in Oslo on the margins of the 3rd India-Nordic Summit in May.

Mr. Kivikoski also referred to the visits to Finland by India's External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal during the summer. "We see India as a trusted partner when it comes to the Indo-Pacific area," he said.
The Ambassador said the India-Finland relationship was increasingly moving beyond conventional trade towards a partnership involving investments and people-to-people exchanges.

"What we are seeing already, and what is happening between the European Union and India and between India and Finland, is that we are now talking about partnership. It's not anymore about me selling something to you and you selling something to me," he said.

"There are more and more Finnish companies coming to the Indian market and more and more Indian companies going to the Finnish market. And of course we hope, and we are confident, that this dynamism will continue in the future," he said.

Bilateral trade in goods and services between India and Finland stood at around $3.7 billion in 2025-26, marking a growth of about 25% over the previous year, and a 38.5% rise from $2.64 billion in 2021-22.
The startup event, Polar Bear Pitching, originated in Oulu, northern Finland, and has expanded internationally, connecting startups with investors and business networks.

articles.title: What does EPFO’s Systematic Withdrawal Plan entail for retirees | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The Story So Far: The Central Board of Trustees (CBT) of the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), in a meeting held in New Delhi on November 19, 2026 approved the Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) for EPF members, enabling periodic payouts of retirement savings. As per the proposed SWP, upon retirement or superannuation, a member will have several options to receive the accumulated PF corpus or a part through periodic withdrawals instead of a lump-sum withdrawal.

As of now, a retiring PF subscriber generally withdraws the entire provident fund accumulation as a lump sum. The proposal, cleared by the CBT, say an eligible member, upon retirement, may opt to receive their provident fund accumulations as monthly withdrawals; quarterly withdrawals; half-yearly withdrawals; or annual withdrawals. The remaining corpus will be invested within the EPF Fund and will continue to earn EPF interest on the running balance. The SWP scheme also proposes to provide flexible options to the member for enhancing his or her corpus in PF by voluntary contributions through payroll, direct additional contributions other than payroll and third-party micro-contributions.

articles.title: Infra push and low base effect pushes core sector growth to series-high of 10.9% in October 2026
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Growth in the core industrial sectors of the economy climbed to a series-high of 10.9% in October 2026, driven by a surge in electricity generation, and coal, cement, and iron ore production, and a low base effect, official data released on Friday (November 20, 2026) showed.

Data released by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on the Index of Core Industries shows that growth in October surpassed the 8.2% in September, the previous series high. The new index, released this year with a base year of 2022-23, has data that goes back only up to April 2024.
However, the data also shows that the strong growth figure in October was also likely aided by the fact that the index grew a relatively poor 0.8% in October last year.

“While core output surged by 10.9% in October 2026, the fastest pace in the new series, this was supported by a low base related to the shift in the festive calendar, with output having expanded by a marginal 0.8% in the year ago month,” Aditi Nayar, chief economist at ICRA said.

“While the growth print for October 2026 signals a strong start for the third quarter of FY2027, this is largely optical,” Ms. Nayar added. “The average performance for October-November 2026 would provide a better assessment, as this would adjust for festive base effects.”

Within the index, the coal sector saw growth accelerating to 23.05% in October 2026, far faster than the 10.7% registered in September. October’s performance, however, is likely also due to low base effect, since the sector contracted 8.4% in October last year.

The growth in the index, however, is in line with what the industry itself has reported. Coal India, the country’s largest coal company, reported that production increased about 19% to 67.2 million tonnes (MT) in October.

A major reason for the growth in coal production was likely demand from the power sector, which saw electricity generation jump by 21.6% in October 2026, up from 12.6% in the previous month. However, this sector too could have benefited from a low base effect, since it contracted nearly 7% in October 2025.
Within the index, the infrastructure-related sectors were the only ones that grew strongly without the aid of a statistical low base effect.

The iron ore sector, for example, grew at a three-month high of 23.4% in October 2026, compared to 18.4% in September and 8.7% in October last year. One of the factors driving this strong growth was that steel production grew at 7.3% in October, the fastest rate in seven months.
The cement sector also grew at a series-high of 15.4% in October 2026, compared to 10.1% in September, and 5.2% in October last year.
The fuel-related sectors in the Index other than coal continued to perform relatively poorly.

articles.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties resume talks to form Israel government
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The parties of caretaker Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot launched a new round of talks on Sunday (November 22, 2026) over whether to form a coalition government, with Mr. Netanyahu’s party insisting on keeping his main policies.

Delegations from Mr. Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud began their meeting at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, an AFP journalist on the scene said, following a first round of talks on Sunday (November 15, 2026).

A former Chief of Staff of the army, Mr. Eisenkot has until December 6, 2026, to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after the October 2026 elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.

His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties, or a national unity government with Likud.
Mr. Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men, a mechanism already tried in Israel.

Such an arrangement could allow him to keep his political protection against the corruption charges he faces, as well as continue to oppose the creation of an independent commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023.

But that prospect runs up against Mr. Eisenkot’s refusal to serve in a cabinet led by Mr. Netanyahu, against whom he centred his campaign. His ally, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, also reiterated on Saturday (November 21, 2026) his refusal to join a coalition with “Netanyahu or his bloc, under any circumstances”.

On Saturday (November 21, 2026), Yashar presented the resumption of talks as “a genuine commitment to forming the broadest possible government”, saying Mr. Eisenkot had asked his representatives to explore all options. But Likud immediately laid down several conditions for its participation in a unity government, a formula backed by Mr. Netanyahu.

Among other things, it demands an end to “all personal attacks and incitement to hatred” targeting the outgoing Prime Minister and his government. It also called for bringing together “all the parties that support the existence of the State of Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people”, without the participation of Arab parties. Mr. Netanyahu and his allies regularly target Arab parties, which secured a record 19 seats in the legislature and are opposed to his remaining in power.

Likud is also demanding agreement on several major policy positions, notably rejecting the creation of a Palestinian state, maintaining Israeli control over territories in Syria, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip, and a compromise on conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews, a particularly sensitive issue in Israel.

On Friday (November 20, 2026), Mr. Eisenkot warned that he would not allow the talks to drag on, saying he was ready to submit to parliament an “emergency national government”. Although he did not spell out how, his statements suggest a two-stage plan: the swift formation of a minority government based on the core opposition parties, and then broadening it.

A minority Eisenkot government could receive support from the 19 Arab party lawmakers, but his right-wing ally Avigdor Liberman rejects working with them, and instead advocates an alliance with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.

articles.title: Ex-U.K. PM Theresa May tells successor to ‘move on’ from Brexit
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Former British Prime Minister Theresa May said she was “aghast” that her successor could be considering rejoining the European Union, and urged him to “move on” from Brexit, in comments broadcast on Sunday (November 22, 2026).

Ms. May’s remarks came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the EU’s top officials on Friday (November 20, 2026) sealed deals at a Brussels summit to ease trade and youth mobility. A decade after Britain narrowly voted to leave the bloc, Mr. Burnham has re-energised talk of closer ties ahead of a government 10-year plan for the U.K., set to be unveiled next month.

Ms. May warned that negotiations with the EU risked taking up vast amounts of government time, hampering efforts to tackle other issues. “And that’s one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU,” she said.

Ms. May, who supported remaining in the 27-member bloc, said government had to respect the result of the 2016 referendum. “When I became prime minister, I was very clear. People have voted for Brexit. We should deliver Brexit,” she told BBC television.

“He (Burnham) wants to pat them (voters) on their head and say ‘you know what? Remember that vote? Well you got it wrong, didn’t you? So have another go and come up with the right answer’,” she said. Ms. May was forced to quit in May 2019 after failing to get her Brexit deal through parliament.

“My message to him (Burnham) really is: People voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on,” she added. Mr. Burnham, who has been in office since July 2026, has committed to his predecessor Keir Starmer’s “red lines” on Europe for this parliament, meaning no return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement. But pro-Brexit campaigners fear he will push at some point to rejoin the 27-nation grouping.
Europe Minister Hamish Falconer said the world had changed since 2016, and the U.K. needed to “think over the long term about our relationship with Europe”.

“That’s why the prime minister is going to set out more next month as part of the 10-year plan about the long-term relationship between the UK and the EU,” he told Sky News . But he insisted the British people “are going to be the boss of every stage of this”.
“We are talking, as the prime minister was clear, about the long term. We will have a general election before then. People will be able to express their views,” he said.
Following Mr. Burnham’s EU deals, legislation to allow the U.K. to align with certain EU rules, including on food standards, is due to be introduced in parliament this week.

articles.title: Nvidia faces U.S. accounting probe amid deepening turmoil: media
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: U.S. securities regulators are investigating the accounting practices of Nvidia, according to U.S. media, adding to the turmoil engulfing the artificial intelligence chip giant following the resignation of its chief executive.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) inquiry is in its early stages, The New York Times reported on Saturday (November 21, 2026), citing people briefed on the confidential investigation. The Wall Street Journal reported on the investigation earlier this week, although it was unable to establish its precise focus. The probe could end without any charges being brought against the company.

Questions about Nvidia’s financial disclosures have intensified amid scrutiny of its dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company investigated by American authorities over suspected shipments of restricted AI chips to China. Nvidia last year changed how it reported sales by geographical location, switching from customers’ billing addresses to the countries where they are headquartered, U.S. media reported.

The change removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown, despite the company’s significant business there. It remains unclear whether the SEC investigation is connected to those accounting changes or to the scandal surrounding former chief executive Jensen Huang.

Mr. Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of working for Beijing. China has denied the espionage allegations, while Megaspeed has maintained that it operates lawfully.
Nvidia’s board has appointed former chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive, and launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding Mr. Huang’s departure.

The upheaval has shaken investor confidence in one of the world’s most valuable companies, whose advanced semiconductors have been central to the global AI boom. Nvidia shares plunged 14% on Friday (November 20, 2026), bringing their losses for the week to more than 20%.

U.S. President Donald Trump nevertheless called on Friday (November 20, 2026) for Mr. Huang to be reinstated. “I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance,” Mr. Trump told reporters. But Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones has ruled out his return, saying board directors unanimously accepted his resignation.

articles.title: Iran strike wounds two in Bahrain, Riyadh denounces ‘criminal’ attacks
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Bahrain on Sunday (November 22, 2026) said two people were wounded in an Iranian attack on Saturday (November 21, 2026) against “a civilian industrial site” in the kingdom, which has repeatedly come under attack in recent days.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards have repeatedly said they targeted U.S. facilities in Bahrain, where Iranian strikes resumed on November 13 after a lull since early September.
“In the wake of the criminal Iranian attacks suffered yesterday (Saturday) by the Kingdom of Bahrain... a Bahraini national with a disability was wounded,” Bahrain’s Interior Ministry said on X.
“His condition is stable. A Pakistani resident was also wounded and is in critical condition. Both are being treated in hospital.”
Two residents told AFP they had seen smoke rising above Sitra Island, east of Manama, which hosts several industrial facilities, including a refinery operated by the state-owned oil company Bapco.

In a statement carried by Iranian state media on Saturday evening, the Revolutionary Guards said they had attacked with missiles and drones U.S. Patriot air defence systems at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, in response to the “continued violations of the airspace” of the Islamic Republic.
Tehran said on Saturday it had intercepted a U.S. drone targeting Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic maritime corridor at the heart of the war in West Asia.

Bahrain’s powerful neighbour Saudi Arabia on Sunday lambasted Tehran for its continued “brutal aggression” against Gulf countries. In a statement published on X, the Saudi Foreign Ministry expressed “the strongest condemnation and denunciation by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia of the criminal Iranian attacks against a civilian industrial facility in the brotherly Kingdom of Bahrain”.

Saudi Arabia also announced early on Sunday that it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis in the west of the kingdom. The region is home to key energy infrastructure, including the oil terminal at the port of Yanbu, as well as the Jizan refinery, located in the far southwest of the country, near the border with Yemen.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighbouring Yemen’s civil war this summer, the latest front in the West Asia war.

Later on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen said it had “intercepted and destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis” toward the greater Riyadh region, which is regularly shaken by explosions.

Since the conflict in Yemen resumed in July, the Houthis have multiplied attacks on Saudi Arabia, particularly since October, targeting its major oil installations and airports in particular. They have also repeatedly struck the financial district of the capital, Riyadh.

articles.title: COP 31 talks fail as EU, others reject any climate deal without language on a fossil fuel phase-out
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: A standoff on a fossil fuel phase-out prevented countries at COP 31, the United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkiye, from achieving any consensus agreement on future climate action on Sunday (November 22, 2026), despite the conference running a record 48 hours into overtime.

The European Union led objections to COP 31 President Murat Kurum’s consensus cover text that failed to include any explicit language about moving away from fossil fuels. The EU’s stance was reportedly supported by about 130 countries.

On the other side of the divide, India is among the nations that supported the proposed cover text, as they want to keep using fossil fuels for the foreseeable future, with Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav stressing that “climate ambition must go hand in hand with means of implementation.”

“We express profound disappointment with the final draft COP31 cover decision or Antalya Pact. At a point where the world urgently needs action to avert disastrous levels of global warming, the draft cover decision falls well short,” Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said, speaking on behalf of the EU.

“We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5 degrees back to within reach… We will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel,” he added.

A cover text is an overarching political decision that frames the outcome of a climate conference rather than settling any single agenda item. It is usually finalised last, and like every outcome, it needs the consensus of all parties.

Panama also formally objected to the text, saying that as a country battling droughts and other perilous impacts of climate change, the lack of any commitment to keep the rise in temperatures below 1.5 degrees C with firm action on phasing out fossil fuels was “a setback”.

“Panama cannot support this decision. One, because it repeats previously agreed commitments without closing the gap between reality and what science demands. Two, because it weighs too much upon technologies such as CCUS [carbon capture utilisation and storage] instead of calling for deep changes, and three, because it weakens language agreed in previous decisions. This is a setback, a rollback,” said Ana Aguilar, Panama’s chief climate negotiator.

On the other side, Saudi Arabia, China, and India are among the countries that are against explicit language on fossil fuel and expressed comfort with the way the cover text language was framed, while also expressing misgivings about the lack of clarity on adaptation finance. The countries are part of the Like Minded Developing Countries (LMDC) coalition, who are insistent on the use of fossil fuel in the foreseeable future to further their economies, but have also significantly deployed renewable energy.

Indian Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav said that India’s voice had shaped the draft COP 31 outcome, especially on food security, livelihoods, and cultural practices recognised in action on methane. However, in a post on X, he emphasised that “climate ambition must go hand in hand with means of implementation. Energy transitions must be nationally determined, just and equitable, backed by finance, technology and capacity-building for developing countries.”

Amandeep Garg, who was leading India’s delegation but speaking in his capacity as a spokesperson on behalf of the LMDC, said on the floor: “Everyone has worked tirelessly, and despite our discomfort with some elements of the text, we are willing to move forward, and continue to engage.” The LMDC expressed “concern” about the principles of equity and common but differentiated responsibility not being adequately reflected, adding that there was a “dilution” of the principle of developed countries taking historical responsibility and meeting their obligations.

“At the threshold of crossing 1.5 deg. C, we have raised a fundamental point – we need to reflect why we are here. Whose emissions, both past and continuing, have exhausted the global carbon budget? The cover decision does not reflect this, and only repeats agreed paragraphs from previous decisions to reflect responsibility and does not connect this with the imminent prospect of exceeding 1.5 deg. C,” he said.

articles.title: Drone strikes hit homes, UN premises in Sudan's capital
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: “Drones struck Sudan 's capital Khartoum, damaging residential homes and a United Nations building on Sunday (November 22, 2026),” witnesses and the world organisation said.

Explosions were heard in the area around Khartoum airport and other parts of the city from at around 2 a.m. until approximately 4:30 a.m. (0000-0230 GMT). A drone strike completely destroyed a house, a witness said, while a Sudanese Army source said the drones had been launched from Ethiopia.

"The drone attack at dawn today is a continuation of Ethiopian aggression against Sudanese territory, as the drones were launched from Ethiopia's Bahir Dar airport," the source told AFP . Sudan has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of allowing attacks to be launched from its territory, a claim Addis Ababa has denied.

Another witness reported that a drone hit the home of a mosque's muezzin, the person who calls Muslims to prayer, in Jebel Aulia, around 45 km (28 miles) south of Khartoum. "People were trying to rescue family members trapped under the rubble," the witness added.

The UN meanwhile said that "a UN premises with UN colleagues in the building was damaged". "This occurred in a civilian neighbourhood," the UN's Humanitarian Office (OCHA) said in a statement posted on X.
OCHA condemned the risk posed to humanitarian workers, saying it was "unacceptable" that UN personnel were being exposed to such danger. Authorities did not immediately report on casualties.

The conflict, which erupted in April 2023 between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Army, has killed more than 2,00,000 people, aid workers estimate, and triggered the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.
The United Nations has repeatedly criticised both sides' rampant use of drones, which killed more than 1,100 people in the first half of 2026.

“Of the hundreds of child casualties this year, two-thirds were killed or injured by drone strikes,” the UN said last week. A Sudanese Army drone strike killed 15 people, including four children, in a West Kordofan village days ago, as the Army pushed through the state, recapturing territory from the RSF.

The rival forces have for the last year wrestled for control of the resource-rich southern Kordofan region, which connects the Army-held centre and east to RSF-controlled Darfur. In recent months, both the Army and the RSF have increasingly relied on drones capable of striking targets hundreds of kilometres away without risking their fighters.

articles.title: Indian science needs fewer borders
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Modern science rightly prides itself on independent scrutiny, irrespective of where the scrutiniser is located. There is no reason seeking the assessment of someone outside India has to constitute colonialism. Yet this was the charge in a widely debated article by Sanjeev Sanyal, Satvik Dev, and Payal Sharma, respectively a Member, the Joint Director, and a Young Professional on the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister.

Researchers write up a study and submit it as a manuscript to a journal. Editors at the journal assess the manuscript and send it out to other experts in the field, asking if the work is worth publishing, or needs to be revised or rejected. If the journal accepts the paper, it will be published, brought to the attention of scientists worldwide, and have a permanent record of it preserved.

articles.title: Thumba to Kourou, over 60 years of space partnership
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: For over 60 years, France and India have shared one of the longest-standing and most trusted space partnerships in the world. At a time when the international environment has become increasingly complex, this partnership matters more than ever before.

Since 1998, their strategic partnership has reposed on defence cooperation — from the Alouette III/Chetak and Rafale aircraft to Scorpène submarines built in India — and people-to-people ties, expanding over time to include artificial intelligence, the blue economy, and much more. What is remarkable about their special global strategic partnership is that, at the core of their national security doctrine, they both share the concept of strategic autonomy. Strategic autonomy does not mean isolating oneself from partners. On the contrary, it means building up one’s own capacities, own analysis, and own decision-making process to be a useful and reliable partner. France has consistently backed India’s rise as a global power, including its permanent seat at the UN Security Council.

articles.title: Paper tiger: on the Green India Mission
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: That all was not well with the Green India Mission was clear even before its approval. After the UPA-I government announced it in 2008, the Ministry of Rural Development had objected to its financial design much before the Union Cabinet approved it in 2014. But the Environment Ministry proceeded anyway and retained largely the same arrangement when it revised the Mission in 2021. Following the Comptroller and Auditor General’s report, on November 19, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) upbraided the Ministry for the Mission’s virtual failure and for still not having issued the implementation guidelines for the revised form. The original 10-year vision was to expand forest and tree cover by 5 million hectares (mha), improve forest quality on another 5 mha, improve forest-related livelihoods for 3 million households, and sequester up to 60 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. The outlay was ₹46,000 crore. In 2014, the Cabinet approved ₹13,000 crore for 1.4 mha each of the first two objectives by 2018, but to be supported to the tune of 81.5% by Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA), National Afforestation Programme (NAP), and MGNREGS funds. In 2021-22, the Ministry folded the NAP into the Mission and, in mid-2025, unveiled a revised version with an allocation of ₹12,190 crore to improve forest cover on 25 mha by 2030, including 24 mha through other schemes. The government had thus expanded the primary target but left the Mission responsible for only 1 mha.

Together with the CAMPA, NAP, and MGNREGS funds never materialising, it is no surprise that the programmes to improve forest quality and forest cover have respectively fallen short by 91.8% and 97.5% vis-à-vis the 2014 target. The Environment Ministry had assembled a large programme around resources that it knew it could not control. Pro-climate work in practice ought to span government schemes to deliver action and justice, and the Ministry ought to have formalised the division of responsibilities and accounting system. The PAC’s new demand that the Ministry submit an implementation timetable is insufficient. From the Jal Shakti Abhiyan in 2019 to the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan in 2024, the government has often floated new programmes banking significantly on funds from existing schemes — an untenable policy when the latter also have their own obligations. And if the VB-G RAM G scheme was to also advance climate justice, the government should not have undermined the erstwhile demand-driven funding model and shifted more financial responsibility to the States. Climate action has to be timely, for which the Union government must dedicate adequate resources and proactively ensure that its initiatives are implemented.

articles.title: Giving India’s first practising woman doctor her due: Kadambini Ganguly​
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: As far as trailblazers go, Kadambini Ganguly will figure right on top of several lists. She was a pioneering woman physician, the first to practise successfully in India, a gynaecologist and a social reformer who, equally efficiently, managed a large family as well. The story of Kadambini Ganguly is one of extraordinary achievement, and if told widely, will continue to inspire the young women of today.

In a profile published in Cureus in 2024, the authors point to the influence of the progressive Bramho Samaj movement, initiated by Raja Ram Mohan Roy, that helped Kadambini emerge from the shackles of conservative orthodoxy that might have stiffled her immense talent. “This environment, which championed the values of education and gender equality, contributed significantly to shaping her exemplary career and lifelong dedication to social justice,” the article reads. Records of her life acknowledge that she was partly recognised during her lifetime, but also mercilessly criticised and defamed for being a progressive, working woman. The full recognition of her contributions in medicine and the social sector came much later, only in recent decades.

articles.title: Why a shortage of clinical psychologists in Keralam govt hospitals is leaving people with intellectual disabilities waiting for certificates
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: People with intellectual disabilities in Keralam are struggling to obtain and renew disability certificates due to a severe shortage of clinical psychologists in government hospitals to conduct Intelligence Quotient (IQ) assessment tests.

As per the latest disability assessment guidelines issued by the Union government’s Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, differently-abled children must undergo assessment tests at least thrice before they turn 18 to obtain permanent disability certificates. During all these assessment phases, an IQ test is a must. However, there are only 22 clinical psychologists under the Directorate of Health Services (DHS) and the Directorate of Medical Education (DME) put together – 17 under the DHS and the rest under the DME.

articles.title: In Keralam, the children beyond healthcare
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Between the pages of a logbook recording Dakshina’s treatment are ₹100, ₹50, ₹20, and ₹10 notes. Dakshina’s mother, Minnal Rani, had filed them away for her daughter’s medical expenses. The child is gone, but the money remains untouched. “We will never spend it,” she says, fighting back tears.

Dakshina was five months old when doctors detected a hole in her heart. Born on June 13, 2025, she was taken to many hospitals, including one in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam’s capital. With surgery ruled out, she was eventually referred to a cooperative hospital at Perinthalmanna, in Malappuram district, a two-and-a-half-hour drive away from home. She died here, on April 13, 2026.
Rani and her husband Chandra Sekhar say the hospital refused to release their daughter’s body until they paid a bill of ₹10,000. They managed to raise the money with the help of a ward councillor.
“We buried her under that tree,” says Rani, pointing to a coconut tree near their house at Vechapathi hamlet in Sholayur panchayat of Attappadi, Palakkad district.

Dakshina’s death is among a series of 10 infant deaths reported this year from Attappadi, a predominantly tribal settlement. There have been four back-to-back deaths in October. Of the 10 infant deaths, six involved congenital anomalies, with heart defects among the commonly reported conditions. An expert committee of doctors and researchers is examining the deaths.

articles.title: Core accountability: On core sector performance
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The core sector performance in October is a good example of how statistical distortions can create incorrect assessments of the economy. The 10.9% growth rate, a series high, has been celebrated as a sign of the Indian economy’s strength and resilience. There is, no doubt, an aspect of this has been reflected in the numbers, especially to do with infrastructure creation. However, the much more impactful factor behind the high core sector growth was a low base effect. The overall Index of Core Industries grew just 0.8% in October 2025 and so, in relation, the performance in October 2026 looked that much faster. This low base effect is even starker when looking at individual sectors within the index. The coal sector grew at a blistering 23% in October, more than twice its growth rate in the previous month. Yet, a large part of this was propelled by the fact that the sector had contracted nearly 8.5% last October. The rest of the sector’s growth was driven by demand of the electricity and iron ore sectors, or so the data show. The electricity sector also grew at a series high of nearly 22% in October, but on the back of a near-7% contraction in October last year. This base effect anomaly is likely down to the fact that the festive season starts at different but similar points every year. As such, a more accurate reading of the economy will be possible once the data for November are available.

The construction-related sectors seem to have seen genuine growth, a reflection of the government’s ongoing infrastructure push. The iron ore sector’s growth rate accelerated to a three-month high of 26.4% in October 2026 as compared to a growth of 8.7% in the same month last year. Steel grew at 7.3% versus 9.5% last year, and cement by 15.4% versus 5.2%. The economy’s dependence on government spending is not going to ease in the near future, and might even intensify as higher costs eat into companies’ profit margins. The core sector data once again highlighted a major reason for these higher costs — the oil and gas sectors. The crude oil sector shrank by 4.1%, its 22nd consecutive month of contraction. The natural gas sector, similarly, contracted 7.6%, a series-worst performance and the 28th straight month of contraction. A major reason behind high inflation in India is the underperformance of these two sectors and the resultant dependence on imported fuel. It is time the Petroleum Ministry candidly explains — to Parliament in December or to the public directly — why India’s fuel output has been continuously falling. If it is a matter of a lack of resources underground, that is one thing, but the underperformance of oil and gas public sector undertakings is quite another. Accountability needs to be set.

articles.title: Paper tiger: On the Green India Mission
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: That all was not well with the Green India Mission was clear even before its approval. After the UPA-I government announced it in 2008, the Ministry of Rural Development had objected to its financial design much before the Union Cabinet approved it in 2014. But the Environment Ministry proceeded anyway and retained largely the same arrangement when it revised the Mission in 2021. Following the Comptroller and Auditor General’s report, on November 19, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) upbraided the Ministry for the Mission’s virtual failure and for still not having issued the implementation guidelines for the revised form. The original 10-year vision was to expand forest and tree cover by 5 million hectares (mha), improve forest quality on another 5 mha, improve forest-related livelihoods for 3 million households, and sequester up to 60 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. The outlay was ₹46,000 crore. In 2014, the Cabinet approved ₹13,000 crore for 1.4 mha each of the first two objectives by 2018, but to be supported to the tune of 81.5% by Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA), National Afforestation Programme (NAP), and MGNREGS funds. In 2021-22, the Ministry folded the NAP into the Mission and, in mid-2025, unveiled a revised version with an allocation of ₹12,190 crore to improve forest cover on 25 mha by 2030, including 24 mha through other schemes. The government had thus expanded the primary target but left the Mission responsible for only 1 mha.

Together with the CAMPA, NAP, and MGNREGS funds never materialising, it is no surprise that the programmes to improve forest quality and forest cover have respectively fallen short by 91.8% and 97.5% vis-à-vis the 2014 target. The Environment Ministry had assembled a large programme around resources that it knew it could not control. Pro-climate work in practice ought to span government schemes to deliver action and justice, and the Ministry ought to have formalised the division of responsibilities and accounting system. The PAC’s new demand that the Ministry submit an implementation timetable is insufficient. From the Jal Shakti Abhiyan in 2019 to the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan in 2024, the government has often floated new programmes banking significantly on funds from existing schemes — an untenable policy when the latter also have their own obligations. And if the VB-G RAM G scheme was to also advance climate justice, the government should not have undermined the erstwhile demand-driven funding model and shifted more financial responsibility to the States. Climate action has to be timely, for which the Union government must dedicate adequate resources and proactively ensure that its initiatives are implemented.

articles.title: Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Initial Public Offering (IPO) of Anthropic , PBC is a mile marker in the arms race to develop superintelligent systems driven by generative AI . Traders valued the firm at $1.27 trillion, a denomination that is bound to become more and more familiar in an industry backed by an endless appetite for capital and unprecedented forms of financialisation. Anthropic’s statements emphasise warnings on the safety of its systems and the consequences of unbridled development of advanced systems. In the history of the development of this technology, this PR spin may just be a blip. After all, their testing has led to AI agents that have broken out of sandboxes and infected unsuspecting organisations’ internal systems: a deluge of agentic chaos that is already a reality has led to little signs of the firm backing its words with action. A familiar trend is playing out, with open source LLMs showing frontier capabilities that can back their erratic impulses, appearing in the space of just months, or sometimes weeks. Advocates of pacing the frontier and managing these emerging risks have been marginalised in a way that has little precedent in this century. It is time for governments to get involved, and specifically, for India to raise its voice on these risks, loudly and unequivocally.

While India’s AI industry is nascent, its positions on international forums carry the weight of a sixth of humanity. A mix of cynical calculations and practical considerations have blunted the use of that voice, for example in the U.S.’s hugely destabilising war of choice against Iran, and Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza. In taking a strong position on what could be the defining transformation of this decade, India has little to lose, and a lot to contribute. India’s AI policies are geared towards diffusion and research of helpful capabilities that can trickle down to the common citizen. The capabilities that the Union government and State governments seek to boost by leveraging AI are removed from the frontier research wreaking havoc within the information security profession around the world. Out-of-control AI agents promise, moreover, significant disruption to outdated government and private systems online. While India has little commercial leverage to curb San Francisco’s accelerationism, its voice is sure to be noticed. India’s focus on AI in international fora, such as the AI Impact Summit in Delhi, has been on consensus. This approach must change. India cannot be silent amid a U.S.-China technological race which could lead to catastrophic damage. New Delhi must not allow the U.S. to stop it from pushing for AI safety.

articles.title: Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilateral summit
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The first trilateral summit between the Presidents of China, the U.S. and Russia , held in Shenzhen on November 19, reflected both the changing global order and the leaders’ shared desire to remain engaged with one another in an increasingly unpredictable world. For U.S. President Donald Trump, the summit was a platform where he could push for joint talks between the world’s three largest nuclear powers on reducing nuclear warheads. After the New START treaty between the U.S. and Russia expired in February 2026, Moscow had signalled that it was ready for talks, but Mr. Trump wanted to involve China as well. For President Xi Jinping, the summit reinforced China’s position as a peer competitor to the U.S. While Russia seeks to deepen partnership with China, the U.S. is looking to build strategic stability. And for Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom the West sought to isolate after he launched the invasion of Ukraine, the summit offered a seat at the high table. The decision to start trilateral talks on nuclear arms and the joint declaration, which stated that ‘a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought’, are steps in the right direction. But much will depend on what follows.

Many had compared the meet to the 1945 Yalta Conference, when Russian leader Joseph Stalin, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill met to discuss the future of post-War Europe. But Shenzhen was not a summit of the victors of a major war. This was more about three great powers setting terms of engagement in a changing world. The summit failed to achieve any breakthrough on any of the issues on the agenda — nuclear arms reduction, non-proliferation or the Ukraine war — or even offer a road map for the future. Moreover, it is not clear if the Shenzhen spirit could be sustained in the medium to long-term as another President in the U.S. could take a very different approach towards Russia and China. The three leaders have called for reform of the UN. While it is a welcome move, any attempt to reform the international system and institutions must also involve other powers, particularly rising middle powers such as India, South Africa and Brazil. But the Shenzhen framework could bring greater stability and predictability to great-power relations. This is important given that two of the Big Three are currently waging two separate wars. The leaders should draw up a clear road map for nuclear talks and other key issues outlined in the Shenzhen declaration, with realistic and achievable objectives. Otherwise, the summit would amount to little more than another diplomatic photo-op.

articles.title: Incomplete remedies: On Special Summary Revision of electoral rolls
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Following the Special Summary Revision (SSR) by the Election Commission of India (ECI) in some States that had undergone the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) , mostly in Phases 1 and 2, some 74 lakh names were added onto the electoral rolls. This meant that the electorate in those 13 States, that had shrunk from 49.61 crore to 45.22 crore after the SIR, has now gone up to 45.96 crore. The ECI has extended the SSR to States and UTs in Phase 3. As before, it requires no proof of citizenship or mapping to older rolls, and insists on personal notice before any deletion other than of the dead. It also directs Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) to cross-verify deletions personally wherever they exceed 2% of a polling station’s electors. Draft deletions in Phase 3 of the SIR averaged 17% , and reached 32.8% in Delhi . The ECI also offered another opportunity to electors deleted by the SIR in the seven States and UTs where it is still underway, such as Delhi and Maharashtra, to return to the rolls. Electors who did not return their forms can do so now, explaining the delay, and those who moved within the State can return through the enumeration form with proof of their new address. EROs will process these forms under Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and restore the elector’s old EPIC number.

These “corrective” measures follow the Supreme Court’s observation on October 28 that forcing deleted electors to re-enrol through Form 6, meant for new voters, was an “error”. The ECI’s use of remedies that existed in the registration rules is a tacit admission that it went wrong during the SIR. But the measures are limited. They reach roughly 4.5 crore of the 13.37 crore struck off the draft rolls and do not cover electors who moved out of their States. Electors in States where the SIR has concluded, including Bihar and West Bengal, which have already voted on the SIR rolls, can return only through the SSR, by filing Form 6 as new voters, with fresh EPIC numbers and no record that they were ever on the roll. In essence, the structure of the SIR remains intact. Electors must still provide details from “the last SIR”, and those whose details are unavailable or do not match will be asked for documents in a manner that amounts to a citizenship test. The legality of the ludicrous “logical discrepancy” checks remains unaddressed. The 2002-03 special revision offered a better way. Those who had shifted homes were enumerated door to door at their new addresses. The Supreme Court must direct the ECI to return to that model.

EROs will process these forms under Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and restore the elector’s old EPIC number.
• These “corrective” measures follow the Supreme Court’s observation on October 28 that forcing deleted electors to re-enrol through Form 6, meant for new voters, was an “error”. The ECI’s use of remedies that existed in the registration rules is a tacit admission that it went wrong during the SIR. But the measures are limited. They reach roughly 4.5 crore of the 13.37 crore struck off the draft rolls and do not cover electors who moved out of their States. Electors in States where the SIR has concluded, including Bihar and West Bengal, which have already voted on the SIR rolls, can return only through the SSR, by filing Form 6 as new voters, with fresh EPIC numbers and no record that they were ever on the roll. In essence, the structure of the SIR remains intact. Electors must still provide details from “the last SIR”, and those whose details are unavailable or do not match will be asked for documents in a manner that amounts to a citizenship test. The legality of the ludicrous “logical discrepancy” checks remains unaddressed. The 2002-03 special revision offered a better way. Those who had shifted homes were enumerated door to door at their new addresses. The Supreme Court must direct the ECI to return to that model.

articles.title: Talks without peace: On Russia, Ukraine, U.S. talks
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. earlier this month failed to produce a major breakthrough or bridge the wide gap between Kyiv and Moscow. Yet, they were a good beginning towards finding a political settlement to Europe’s longest war since the Second World War . In the two-day talks, hosted by the U.S., the warring sides agreed on some humanitarian measures, including prisoner exchange. U.S. representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow after the talks to discuss the proposal. In the next stage, U.S., Ukrainian and European officials will meet in Berlin to discuss a coordinated European and Ukrainian position towards the peace process. As of now, Russian and Ukrainian positions remain far apart. Russia demands Ukraine withdraw from the territories of Donbas it still controls to stop attacks. Russia also wants to introduce limits to Ukrainian military capabilities and Kyiv to declare neutrality (give up its NATO ambitions). Ukraine, on the other hand, has rejected making any territorial concessions for a settlement and asked for security guarantees from the West so that Russia would not attack the country again.

That Ukraine survived Russia’s invasion and continued to resist Russian forces for almost five years is no small feat. But it has also paid a huge price for its resistance. The country has lost more than 20% of its territory. Millions have fled, while men of fighting age are being drafted into the military . Ukraine’s economy is kept afloat by European support, while its military continues to rely on NATO for weapons and other supplies. Until recently, the West stood united in its support for Ukraine against Russia, but that unity has since begun to fray. U.S. President Donald Trump, who has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel, is seeking to reset Washington’s ties with Moscow . European leaders, who initially sought to isolate Russia, have also started reestablishing contacts with the Kremlin. In October, Finnish and Norwegian leaders held direct talks with Mr. Putin. To be sure, Ukraine’s long-range strikes can hurt Russia, as the recent attack on the Kerch Bridge demonstrated. But such strikes are unlikely to change the Kremlin’s thinking about the war. As the conflict drags on, Ukraine’s position is weakening, and its allies are growing increasingly divided. After almost five years, Russia has failed to take a decisive victory. Ukraine does not have a credible path towards victory either. A diplomatic settlement, therefore, is the only way forward. The Abu Dhabi talks recognised this reality. But for the process to be meaningful, Europe must also be brought to the negotiating table.

articles.title: Man injured in crocodile attack near Chidambaram

fullParagraphs: A 42-year-old man sustained minor injuries on his left thigh after being bitten by a crocodile that strayed into a house in Koppadi village near Chidambaram on Sunday.

According to police sources, P. Ilavarasan of Koppadi village was staying in his house when a dog began to bark continuously. When he went outside he was shocked to see a crocodile. Forest Department personnel arrived and, with the help of residents, safely captured the crocodile and released it into the Vakkaramari lake in Chidambaram.

articles.title: Pattabiram residents urge Highways dept. to build roundabouton CTH Road junction
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Residents of Pattabiram have urged the Highways Department to build a roundabout on the Chennai–Tiruvallur High Road (CTH) or Chennai–Tirupati–Renigunta Road near the flyover, replacing the Level Crossing 2 on the railway siding.
Without a roundabout, the six-way junction presents a chaotic sight during peak hours, said Roy Rozario, a resident.
Apart from the lanes of the C.T.H Road, road to/from Poonamallee and M.G. Road join the junction. People heading to the police station, TIDEL Park, hotels, schools, and colleges use the junction.

“Due to the lack of a roundabout, a lot of accidents happen as people drive on the wrong side of the road or drive recklessly. Long ago, the government had announced that a roundabout would be constructedat the location. We hope that it would come up soon,” he added.

Residents, meanwhile, have urged the department to open the other side of the flyover to traffic. “It has been completed. Only some works such as lighting, removal of excess cement concrete, and painting seem to remain. Though the surface is rough, people are driving on the incomplete side of the flyover to reach the other side,” said T. Sadagopan, activist.
The space beneath the flyover must also be cleared and the roads must be laid properly.

“Several bus services from Poonamallee, Thiruninravur, and other places have been cut, as there is no space to park the buses. Those buses that start from Pattabiram wait at random spots on the C.T.H Road. We want the Highways to also construct a foot overbridge beneath the flyover, or a limited-use subway,” said a resident.
Sources said the roundabout would be formed during the widening of the road. As far as a subway or a foot overbridge was concerned, necessary studies would be taken up.

articles.title: Six sent to juvenile home after Mumbai assault; Maharashtra SP leader seeks age change
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A juvenile court in Mumbai on Saturday sent six minors to a juvenile correctional home till December 4 in connection with the alleged assault of a couple at a garden in Kurla on Friday evening, police said on Sunday. The six are aged between 12 and 15, the Ghatkopar police said.

Deputy Commissioner of Police Ganesh Shinde said an FIR was lodged against the minors under Sections 189(2) (unlawful assembly), 118(1) (voluntarily causing hurt using dangerous weapons or means), 352 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace), and 351(2) (criminal intimidation) and other relevant provisions of the BNS.
All of them were produced before the Juvenile Justice Board and notices were sent to their parents.

According to the police, the couple was at the garden behind Phoenix Marketcity mall when a group of minors surrounded them and began to abuse them. When the couple tried to reason with the group, they assaulted them with a hockey stick and forced them out of the garden. Police detained them after a video of the incident surfaced on social media.
The police said they are recording the statements of the couple and the juveniles to determine whether the two groups had a dispute before the incident that took place at the Pramod Mahajan Garden.

The incident drew sharp reactions from political parties, with many condemning it. Samajwadi Party Maharashtra president Abu Asim Azmi said the juvenile age threshold should be brought down from 18 to 15 and that those below 18 years who commit murder, robbery or harassment should not be given concessions under the law. Mr. Azmi added that the incident should not be linked to religion and that the law should act without discrimination.
Meanwhile, BJP leader Kirit Somaiya met the couple at the Ghatkopar police station and promised action.

NCP (SP) MP Supriya Sule urged Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, who holds the Home portfolio, to “adopt a no-tolerance policy towards such incidents” and said citizens should be able to move around freely in the State.
Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Intekhab Farooqui also condemned the assault.

articles.title: Over 40% Group A posts vacant at PGIMS Rohtak, says former Minister
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Alleging that 41.6% of the sanctioned Group A posts at the Post-Graduate Institute of Medical Sciences (PGIMS) in Rohtak were lying vacant, former Haryana Home Minister Subhash Batra on Sunday questioned the BJP government’s claims of improving healthcare services in the State.

Citing an inspection by the Assembly’s Subject Committee in February, Mr. Batra said 424 of the 1,018 sanctioned Group A posts at the institute were vacant. He said the shortage of doctors, specialists and healthcare staff was affecting patient care at the institute, which catered to over 8,000 patients daily in its outpatient department.
Manjunath, in-charge of the Public Relations Department, PGIMS, did not respond to repeated calls and messages seeking his response to the former Minister’s allegations.

Addressing a press conference, Mr. Batra also pointed out that only 200 of the 540 medicines on the government-approved list were available in the hospital store during the Health Minister’s inspection in April. Supply orders for 172 types of medicines and surgical materials were pending with companies, he alleged.

Alleging that the “condition of the Radiology Department is also extremely concerning”, Mr. Batra said 10 of the 13 sanctioned faculty posts and nine of the 11 Senior Resident posts were vacant in the department, as per a September-October 2026 report. Of the nearly 500 patients advised ultrasound examinations daily, only 40% could undergo the test on the same day, he added.

Questioning the gap between budgetary allocations and the availability of health care facilities, Mr. Batra said ₹1,232 crore had been allocated to the Pandit Bhagwat Dayal Sharma University of Health Sciences and PGIMS for 2026-27, an increase of ₹422 crore over the previous year, but patients continued to face shortages of medicines and delays in diagnostic tests.
Mr. Batra also raised concerns over two incidents of ceiling plaster falling in the old hospital building in October.

On behalf of the Congress, Mr. Batra demanded that all vacant posts be filled, medicine stocks and pending complaints be made public, diagnostic facilities expanded and old hospital buildings subjected to a safety audit.

“The poor, labourers, farmers and the middle-class families in the State need doctors on time, essential medicines and quality treatment and not speeches and announcements,” he said, adding that the Congress would continue to raise this serious issue concerning health and hold the government accountable.

articles.title: Core accountability: On core sector performance
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The core sector performance in October is a good example of how statistical distortions can create incorrect assessments of the economy. The 10.9% growth rate, a series high, has been celebrated as a sign of the Indian economy’s strength and resilience. There is, no doubt, an aspect of this has been reflected in the numbers, especially to do with infrastructure creation. However, the much more impactful factor behind the high core sector growth was a low base effect. The overall Index of Core Industries grew just 0.8% in October 2025 and so, in relation, the performance in October 2026 looked that much faster. This low base effect is even starker when looking at individual sectors within the index. The coal sector grew at a blistering 23% in October, more than twice its growth rate in the previous month. Yet, a large part of this was propelled by the fact that the sector had contracted nearly 8.5% last October. The rest of the sector’s growth was driven by demand of the electricity and iron ore sectors, or so the data show. The electricity sector also grew at a series high of nearly 22% in October, but on the back of a near-7% contraction in October last year. This base effect anomaly is likely down to the fact that the festive season starts at different but similar points every year. As such, a more accurate reading of the economy will be possible once the data for November are available.

The construction-related sectors seem to have seen genuine growth, a reflection of the government’s ongoing infrastructure push. The iron ore sector’s growth rate accelerated to a three-month high of 26.4% in October 2026 as compared to a growth of 8.7% in the same month last year. Steel grew at 7.3% versus 9.5% last year, and cement by 15.4% versus 5.2%. The economy’s dependence on government spending is not going to ease in the near future, and might even intensify as higher costs eat into companies’ profit margins. The core sector data once again highlighted a major reason for these higher costs — the oil and gas sectors. The crude oil sector shrank by 4.1%, its 22nd consecutive month of contraction. The natural gas sector, similarly, contracted 7.6%, a series-worst performance and the 28th straight month of contraction. A major reason behind high inflation in India is the underperformance of these two sectors and the resultant dependence on imported fuel. It is time the Petroleum Ministry candidly explains — to Parliament in December or to the public directly — why India’s fuel output has been continuously falling. If it is a matter of a lack of resources underground, that is one thing, but the underperformance of oil and gas public sector undertakings is quite another. Accountability needs to be set.
